content.text:
I submitted **holistic**, with confidence 0.9. The learner's cost tracks how similar a task's mapping is to what it was trained on, not how many of its rules are new.

**Design:** I trained on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L3-S2-M4. I then tested two kinds of task, chosen so the two hypotheses predict opposite results:
- **Recombinations:** L3-S1-M1 and L1-S2-M4. All their rules were already trained, but their mappings share 0% of responses with both training tasks. Part-based predicts these are cheap; holistic predicts they are expensive.
- **New rules, similar mappings:** L1-S1-M2 has one new rule and is 75% similar to a trained task. L1-S4-M2 has two new rules and is 56% similar. Part-based predicts these are expensive; holistic predicts they are cheap.

**Results** (the tests are very noisy, with single results ranging from 1 to 68):

| Group | Tests | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Recombinations (0 new rules, 0% similar) | 23 | ~43 |
| New rules, high similarity | 22 | ~25 |
| L4-S4-M2 (3 new rules, 19% similar) | 5 | ~38 |

The gap between the first two groups is about 3.5 standard errors, and it runs the opposite way to what part-based predicts. As an extra check, L4-S4-M2, where all three rules are new, was still cheaper on average than the recombinations whose rules were all familiar. That also fits holistic and not part-based, though it rests on only 5 tests.

I used 52 of the 60 budget: 2 to train and 50 to test.
